title: Default-cost reinforcement with carbon-steel behavior and no corrosion in ordinary exposures

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reinforcing bar that ordinary concrete construction could buy and use much like carbon-steel rebar, while gaining the corrosion resistance now associated with specialty reinforcement. It would retain comparable stiffness, yielding behavior, elongation, ductility, bending and detailing capability, and structural performance in fire. Its feedstocks and manufacturing process would support reinforcing-steel volumes, and its installed first cost would fall within the regional carbon-steel reinforcement price band. This is a proposed combination of capabilities, not an achievement demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

Existing alternatives explain the target. Stainless reinforcement offers corrosion resistance but has historically carried a substantial initial-cost premium and does not automatically reproduce carbon steel’s stress–strain behavior. Fiber-reinforced polymer, or FRP, bars avoid steel corrosion but are anisotropic, remain elastic until failure, and require design procedures that account for limited ductility. CIV-11 seeks corrosion resistance together with familiar yielding-steel structural behavior and ordinary first cost.

For this concept, ordinary exposures would need explicit engineering definitions: specified chloride conditions, carbonation conditions, and stray-current conditions wherever resistance to them is claimed. The title’s ambition of no corrosion should be interpreted operationally through declared detection limits, exposure durations, and retained structural performance. A successful bounded demonstration would not establish thermodynamic immunity in every environment.

significance.text: Reinforcement corrosion can reduce load-bearing capacity, damage the bond between bar and concrete, and contribute to cracking and cover spalling. Suppressing that deterioration while retaining ordinary steel design behavior would address a major service-life constraint of reinforced concrete. The benefit would extend beyond preserving bar area: the reinforcement and concrete must continue to act together as a structural member.

Conditional engineering synthesis: if the full combination were achieved at carbon-steel first cost, corrosion-resistant reinforcement could become an ordinary construction choice rather than a selective premium purchase. Qualifying marine, de-icing, and carbonating exposures could see longer service and less corrosion-driven repair without sacrificing familiar ductile design. Affordable resistance to specified stray-current conditions could offer a similar benefit where those conditions occur. Actual service-life gains would depend on the exposure, concrete system, construction quality, and demonstrated durability.

Those benefits would not establish unlimited structural life or automatically justify less concrete cover. Cover also serves bond, structural, and fire functions; reducing it would require separate qualification and applicable code acceptance. The reviewed discussion of cover relaxation does not support an unconditional reduction. Likewise, introducing improved reinforcement into new construction does not solve the practical problem of replacing bars inside already contaminated existing members.

The economic scale of corrosion provides broad context. Koch and coauthors’ 2016 IMPACT study estimated the worldwide cost of all corrosion at US$2.5 trillion, equivalent to 3.4% of 2013 world GDP. The estimate extrapolated from five older national studies: India in 2011–2012, the United States in 1998, Japan in 1997, Kuwait in 1987, and the United Kingdom in 1970. It is not a reinforced-concrete cost total. The study’s estimated 15–35% savings from available corrosion-control practices concerns practices already known, not savings attributable to this proposed bar.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central engineering challenge is to combine affordability, scalable production, corrosion resistance, and carbon-steel-like mechanical behavior in the same reinforcement system. The supplied evidence establishes why this combination matters, but does not establish whether it remains commercially unavailable in November 2026. High corrosion resistance alone is insufficient: the 2022 stainless-reinforcement review describes a continuous nonlinear stress–strain response without a clear yield point, illustrating why a corrosion-resistant metal does not automatically satisfy the proposed yield-plateau requirement.

The material must also work as reinforcement inside concrete. Suitable bond, anchorage, bending behavior, crack control, and composite action must accompany the required stiffness, elongation, and ductility. FRP’s high tensile strength along its fibers does not by itself provide this interchangeability: its anisotropy and elastic-to-failure response change the design philosophy. Corrosion resistance and tensile strength therefore cannot substitute for qualification of the complete structural behavior.

Fire performance is a separate member-level barrier. Bare-bar properties do not establish how a reinforced concrete member will carry load during fire. The 2022 stainless review identified a notable lack of information on stainless-reinforced concrete elements under fire conditions. The supplied ACI educational excerpt also describes increased cracking and deflection at elevated temperatures in FRP-reinforced concrete and advises against its use where fire resistance is essential to structural integrity. These are reasons for explicit fire qualification; they do not establish the present requirements of every applicable code.

Engineering synthesis: the remaining durability and production barriers include defining the environments the bar can withstand, connecting accelerated tests to practical exposure durations, retaining structural performance after exposure, and producing consistent material at competitive installed cost. Stainless resistance is not universal, and FRP can deteriorate through mechanisms other than steel corrosion. The supplied material does not identify a particular composition or manufacturing route that resolves all these constraints.

current_state.text: Rabi, Shamass, and Cashell’s 2022 review, published in Construction and Building Materials, documents stainless-reinforced concrete applications and structural member experiments. It reports stainless reinforcement initial costs typically three to eight times those of conventional steel and describes use concentrated in applications susceptible to chloride ingress, including coastal buildings, tunnels, and bridges. These are historical review findings, not verified 2026 procurement prices or market shares.

The same review describes bridge life-cycle comparisons, including the Öland and Schaffhausen bridges, in which higher initial costs could be offset over decades. Such cases support evaluating whole-life economics in demanding exposures, but do not demonstrate first-cost parity for ordinary buildings. The underlying bridge comparison referenced by the review was not separately inspected in the supplied research. The review also identified gaps in efficient design guidance and long-term cost data; persistence of those gaps through 2026 has not been established here.

The introduction to ACI 440.1R-15 documents successful practical applications of FRP reinforcing bars worldwide over preceding decades. It explains that the bars do not yield, are elastic until failure, and have high tensile strength principally along the reinforcing fibers. Their limited ductility requires different design procedures. The reviewed copy was a five-page preview containing introductory material, not the complete guide, so it cannot support conclusions about all of the guide’s provisions or current code coverage.

An ACI Committee 440 educational excerpt advises against FRP reinforcement where fire resistance is essential to structural integrity. Its date and precise edition were not established, and many slides lacked extracted content. The relevant fire slide was available, but its caution must remain attributed to that teaching material. It is not evidence of an inspected provision in the full guide or a universal present-day prohibition.

None of the supplied texts demonstrates one bar combining carbon-steel first cost, comparable yielding behavior and stiffness, comparable member fire performance, and specialty-level corrosion resistance in ordinary construction. That is a boundary of this evidence set, not proof that no such product exists. The supplied record contains no updated literature, procurement, or code search establishing the position on 2026-11-01; retrieval on that date does not make the underlying 2015 and 2022 technical sources current.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed affordability and scale demonstration: produce bars using feedstocks and a manufacturing route credibly scalable to reinforcing-steel tonnage, with measured production consistency and a credible capacity expansion basis. Real procurement should show an in-place price, without a permanent subsidy, within the regional carbon-steel reinforcing band. Report material, fabrication, installation, and qualification costs sufficiently clearly to compare like-for-like structural work. A bar procurement price no greater than about twice the carbon-steel bar price could be an intermediate affordability milestone; it would not satisfy the central installed first-cost parity objective.
completion_criteria.label: Scalable production with installed carbon-steel cost parity

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mechanical and structural demonstration: under a recognized reinforcing specification, show a yield plateau, elongation, and elastic modulus comparable to the carbon-steel grade being replaced. Demonstrate suitable bending, bond, anchorage, and member behavior so that familiar ductile design assumptions are justified. A representative reinforced member should achieve the same fire rating as the carbon-steel alternative under comparable loading and test conditions. These are proposed qualification requirements, not a claim that an existing specification already endorses the hypothetical material.
completion_criteria.label: Carbon-steel-comparable mechanical and structural performance with matching fire ratings

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability demonstration: for each claimed chloride, carbonation, or stray-current exposure, agree in advance on severity, duration, specimen and member configurations, measurement sensitivity, and acceptance limits. Measure corrosion or section loss together with retained structural performance, including bond where relevant, against an appropriate specialty reinforcement. A result below the detection limit should be reported with that limit. A successful test in one exposure should not be generalized to untested environments, and absence of steel corrosion should not stand in for evidence against other degradation mechanisms.
completion_criteria.label: Exposure-specific corrosion resistance with retained structural performance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and deployment demonstration: reproduce the relevant results across independently tested production batches, publish the test conditions and meaningful failures, and use the bar as primary reinforcement in at least one ordinary building or bridge under the applicable current code, outside a specialty marine pilot. Document practical boundaries such as eligible grades, sizes, fabrication methods, and exposure classes. The deployment count and approximately twofold intermediate price milestone are proposals, not established consensus thresholds. Finite tests and deployments would establish demonstrated breadth, not literal universality or unlimited service life.
completion_criteria.label: Independent batch reproduction and code-compliant ordinary building or bridge deployment

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CIV-05, “Tensile-ductile mineral structures that replace reinforced concrete at ordinary cost,” overlaps in seeking affordable structural performance but targets a different material system. CIV-11 retains the bar-and-concrete architecture and improves its reinforcement; CIV-05 proposes mineral structures capable of replacing reinforced concrete. Their shared affordability and ductility ambitions do not make them the same capability. This distinction follows from the supplied roster titles; detailed CIV-05 requirements were not provided.

Roster-based synthesis: CIV-04, “Repeated recovery of structural load capacity after cracking,” concerns restoring capacity after damage. CIV-11 concerns resistance to reinforcement-corrosion deterioration while retaining steel-like behavior. A corrosion-resistant bar would not by itself demonstrate repeated structural healing, and a crack-recovery system would not by itself establish corrosion-resistant reinforcement. Replacing reinforcement inside an existing contaminated member is another construction challenge that neither title alone resolves.

Roster-based synthesis: CIV-01 addresses a primary binder without process carbon dioxide, while CIV-07 addresses load-bearing engineered living materials. Both could intersect with the concrete or surrounding material used with reinforcement, but neither establishes CIV-11’s combined bar performance and price. CIV-09 targets immediate occupancy after a design earthquake, and CIV-12 targets fail-safe adaptive primary structural response; preserving ductility could contribute to structural design, but corrosion resistance alone would not deliver either system-level outcome. CIV-10’s structural energy-storage function is also distinct from reinforcement durability. These are limited comparisons based on roster titles, not evidence of demonstrated compatibility.

change_log.change: Preserved CIV-11’s identity while defining the target as a combined material, structural, manufacturing, and installed-cost capability.
change_log.reason: The innovation lies in achieving the full combination; existing corrosion-resistant reinforcement does not automatically satisfy it.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical present-day nonavailability with a dated account of the supplied evidence and an explicit 2026 knowledge boundary.
change_log.reason: The 2015 guide preview and 2022 review establish historical context, but the supplied record contains no freshness search confirming current market or code conditions.

change_log.change: Retained the three-to-eightfold stainless initial-cost range and bridge life-cycle examples with their historical and secondary-source limitations.
change_log.reason: Life-cycle cost recovery is useful evidence but does not establish ordinary-building first-cost parity or current procurement prices.

change_log.change: Integrated stainless stress–strain behavior, bond and anchorage requirements, and separate member fire qualification into the technical barriers and proposed demonstrations.
change_log.reason: Corrosion resistance and retained bar area alone do not establish structural interchangeability with carbon-steel reinforcement.

change_log.change: Preserved FRP’s demonstrated applications and mechanical distinctions while narrowing the fire statement to the undated educational excerpt.
change_log.reason: The full ACI guide was not available in the reviewed preview, and the teaching material cannot establish universal current code requirements.

change_log.change: Replaced claims of removing the corrosion clock or dispensing with extra cover with conditional service-life benefits and separate cover qualification.
change_log.reason: Finite exposure tests do not establish unlimited life, and concrete cover also serves bond, structural, and fire functions.

change_log.change: Separated installed first-cost parity from the proposed approximately twofold bar-price milestone and expanded exposure and reproducibility criteria.
change_log.reason: The two price comparisons measure different outcomes, and convincing durability evidence requires defined conditions, detection limits, retained performance, and repeatability.

change_log.change: Retained the IMPACT economic figures, historical extrapolation basis, and available-practice savings estimate with explicit scope limits.
change_log.reason: These provide economic context without assigning all-corrosion costs or existing-practice savings to reinforced concrete or the hypothetical innovation.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster titles to make qualified distinctions with CIV-04, CIV-05, and other directly relevant entries.
change_log.reason: The review lacked these definitions, but the final inputs supply titles sufficient for limited comparisons without inventing detailed requirements or merging concepts.

unresolved_issues: Whether a commercially available reinforcement system satisfies the full combination as of 2026-11-01 remains unresolved; no current literature, procurement, or code survey was supplied.
No candidate composition or manufacturing route is identified, so feedstock sufficiency, production consistency, and competitive installed cost remain unproven.
Exposure severities, test durations, detection limits, acceptable loss, and retained-performance thresholds remain to be defined for each claimed environment.
The approximately twofold bar-price milestone remains a proposed intermediate target, not first-cost parity or an established industry standard.
The current scope of FRP fire acceptance cannot be determined from the five-page guide preview and undated, partly extracted educational excerpt.
The bridge life-cycle comparisons remain secondary reports from the stainless review; the underlying referenced comparison was not separately inspected.
The supplied IMPACT material does not establish a reinforced-concrete share of worldwide corrosion costs.

The review’s recommendation to defer all CIV-04 and CIV-05 comparisons was not adopted in full because the final inputs include their roster titles. Comparisons remain limited to those titles; detailed boundaries and compatibility are unresolved.

brief.title: Rust-resistant reinforcing bars at ordinary steel prices
possible: People could build concrete homes, bridges and other structures with reinforcing bars that resist corrosion—the chemical damage that eats away metal—at the installed price of ordinary steel. The bars would keep steel’s stiffness and ability to stretch under overload while still carrying weight.
why: Corrosion inside concrete can weaken a structure, loosen the grip between bars and concrete, and make concrete crack and break away. Affordable corrosion resistance could mean longer service and fewer repairs for buildings and bridges, while preserving familiar ways of designing them.

sources.showed: They estimated the worldwide cost of corrosion using earlier national studies.
sources.quote: The global cost of corrosion is estimated to be US$2.5 trillion
sources.cited_for: Corrosion imposes a large economic burden across industries.
sources.not_established: The estimate does not isolate reinforced concrete costs or predict savings from these bars.

sources.who: Musab Rabi, Rabee Shamass and K.A. Cashell
sources.showed: Their review describes stainless steel reinforcement in structures and experiments. It documents corrosion resistance alongside higher initial costs and differences in how the metal stretches under load.
sources.quote:
However, it is also more expensive than carbon steel in terms of the initial 
cost and this is one of the primary reasons that it is not specified more commonly in RC applications, and 
tends to be used mainly in harsh and aggressive environments.
sources.cited_for: Stainless steel demonstrates corrosion-resistant reinforcement, with cost and structural behavior still central to the proposed capability.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate ordinary installed cost combined with matching steel behavior and structural fire performance.

sources.showed: The committee describes practical use of fiber-reinforced polymer bars, made from fibers held in plastic. They avoid steel corrosion but need different structural design methods.
sources.quote:
Fiber-reinforced polymer reinforcing bars offer advantages over 
steel reinforcement because they are noncorrosive.
sources.cited_for: Reinforcing bars can avoid steel corrosion while differing substantially from steel in structural behavior.
sources.not_established: These bars do not provide steel’s ability to stretch permanently under overload while continuing to carry load.

sources.showed: The committee’s teaching material describes larger cracks and bending at higher temperatures in concrete reinforced with fiber-reinforced polymer, or FRP.
sources.quote:
FRP materials are characterized as linear elastic to failure and thus have no 
yield point or yield strain value.
sources.cited_for: Corrosion resistance alone does not establish steel-like behavior or adequate performance during fire.
sources.not_established: The teaching material does not establish a universal prohibition on FRP use where fire resistance matters.

shown: The Progresso Pier in Mexico had served for over 70 years without major repair or maintenance, according to Rabi, Shamass and Cashell’s review. It provides a practical example of long service with stainless steel reinforcement.
missing: A bar still needs to demonstrate corrosion resistance, ordinary steel behavior and ordinary installed cost together.
Complete concrete members need matching fire performance and reliable load transfer between bars and concrete.
Durability tests need to establish retained strength and grip in each claimed environment, including resistance to damage other than corrosion.
Consistent production at construction scale needs independent testing and ordinary, code-compliant deployment.

milestones.label: Scalable production at ordinary installed steel cost
milestones.explanation: Production would have to deliver consistent bars at construction scale, with installed costs within local ordinary-steel prices without permanent subsidy. This would make them an affordable routine choice.

milestones.label: Steel-like structural behavior and matching fire ratings
milestones.explanation: Bars and concrete members would have to match steel in stiffness, stretching under steady overload, bending, grip and fire rating. This would support familiar assumptions about how structures carry loads.

milestones.label: Corrosion resistance with retained structural performance
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to meet declared corrosion limits and retain structural performance in each claimed environment, against suitable specialty bars. This would establish where the protection works and its limits.

milestones.label: Independent reproduction and ordinary construction use
milestones.explanation: Independent tests would have to reproduce results across production batches, report failures and support code-compliant use in an ordinary building or bridge. This would connect laboratory performance to routine construction.

uncertain: Whether a commercially available system already meets the full combination remains unresolved.
No candidate material or manufacturing route is identified, leaving affordable production at scale an open question.
Exposure severity, test duration, detection limits and acceptable retained performance still need agreed definitions.

page.title: Corrosion-resistant reinforcement at carbon-steel installed cost
page.definition: Steel reinforcing bars for concrete that meet published chloride-corrosion limits, retain steel stiffness and plastic deformation after yielding, and provide the same member fire rating as carbon steel. Their installed first cost is no greater than carbon-steel reinforcement for matched construction.

goal.need: A 2022 review reports stainless reinforcement initial costs 3–8 times those of conventional steel and describes corrosion-driven inspection, repair and replacement of reinforced-concrete infrastructure. Combining chloride resistance with yielding-steel behaviour and carbon-steel installed first cost would address the material-cost barrier identified in that review.

statements.quote: ensure a corrosion-free design life of 75 to 100 years when exposed to adverse environments.
statements.context: The report describes the objective of FHWA’s Corrosion Resistant Reinforcing for Concrete Components research project, begun in May 1993.

statements.quote: develop and commercialize a new type of steel rebar which resists corrosion but outperforms existing rebar and is cost competitive.
statements.context: The objective appears in SBIR Phase I award 2231660 to Allium Engineering for stainless-steel cladding on carbon steel.

completion.title: A corrosion-resistant steel reinforcing system is installed at no greater first cost than carbon steel.
completion.criterion: A commercially supplied reinforcing system meets the Grade 420 tensile limits and ASTM A955 chloride-corrosion limits below, supports the same approved stiffness, yielding, bond and anchorage assumptions as its carbon-steel comparator, and achieves a 2-hour ASTM E119 floor rating. A matched construction procurement demonstrates installed reinforcement-system first cost no greater than carbon steel for the same location, quantities and scope, including fabrication, delivery, placing, qualification and consequential design costs, with owner acceptance under the project specification.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas, combining published material tests and construction acceptance requirements with an installed-cost comparison.
completion.basis: Searches of FHWA reinforcement programmes, NSF SBIR awards, ASTM and AASHTO specifications, and DOT acceptance documents found no combined endpoint for corrosion resistance, steel interchangeability and installed-cost parity. This Atlas test interprets NSF’s “cost competitive” goal as matched installed-cost parity. The chloride-test boundary, Grade 420 comparator and code-defined 2-hour floor rating specify a bounded demonstration.

milestones.title: Reinforcing bars yield at 420–540 MPa and meet Grade 420 steel strength and elongation limits.
milestones.criterion: Meet ASTM A706M-22a Table 2 Grade 420 tensile limits. Yield strength is 420–540 MPa, tensile strength is at least 550 MPa, and actual tensile/yield strength ratio is at least 1.25. Minimum elongation over 200 mm is 14% for bar Nos. 10, 13, 16 and 19, 12% for Nos. 22, 25, 29, 32 and 36, and 10% for Nos. 43 and 57. Allium claimed ASTM A706-equivalent physical and mechanical characteristics for stainless-clad bars on 30 July 2025 in a press release, not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: ASTM International, ASTM A706/A706M-22a, Table 2. The numerical thresholds appear in a table. This low-alloy-steel specification supplies the mechanical comparator.

milestones.title: Reinforcing bars sustain mean corrosion rates ≤0.25 µm/year through a 15-week chloride test.
milestones.criterion: Meet ASTM A955/A955M-19 Annex A1.2 using the Annex A2 rapid macrocell test in simulated concrete pore solution containing 15% sodium chloride. Throughout testing, the mean corrosion rate of at least five specimens is ≤0.25 µm/year and every specimen is ≤0.50 µm/year. A March 2025 University of Kansas report tested six specimens of 15M 2205 stainless reinforcement from heat RZ 6858 for 15 weeks. Maximum mean corrosion rate was 0.15 µm/year, and every specimen met the individual limit. This industry-sponsored report was not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: ASTM International, ASTM A955/A955M-19, Annex A1.2. The threshold was written for stainless-steel reinforcement.
milestones.threshold_quote: the average corrosion rate for a minimum of five specimens shall at no time during the test exceed 0.25 µm/year

milestones.title: A concrete floor reinforced with the candidate bars achieves a 2-hour fire-resistance rating.
milestones.criterion: A loadbearing floor assembly achieves at least 2 hours under ASTM E119, including load-carrying, heat-transmission and hot-gas criteria applicable to the assembly. This is the floor rating specified for Type I-A and I-B construction in 2018 IBC Table 601. Mehwish et al. (2025) numerically predicted almost 60 minutes more fire resistance with stainless reinforcement at a 0.59% reinforcement ratio than carbon steel at 0.84%, using a model validated against carbon-steel beam fire tests.
milestones.set_by: International Code Council, 2018 IBC Table 601, reproduced in its 2018 IBC Essentials training material. The 2-hour threshold appears in a table for Type I-A and I-B floors. ASTM International supplies test method E119.

milestones.title: Production reinforcement is installed in a highway structure and accepted under its owner's specifications.
milestones.criterion: For the Caltrans route, delivered reinforcement meets the contract’s material requirements, required certificates and mill tests, and placement, hook and splice requirements, and receives resident-engineer acceptance. On 30 July 2025, Allium reported approximately 70,000 lb of stainless-clad reinforcement installed in the Long Valley Creek Bridge deck replacement on U.S. Route 101 in Mendocino County, California. Its press release, not peer reviewed, also reported that Caltrans product evaluation was ongoing.
milestones.set_by: California Department of Transportation, Construction Manual Sections 6-203A(5), 4-5202 and 4-5203. These requirements govern California highway construction acceptance.
milestones.threshold_quote: The resident engineer has the sole responsibility for acceptance of material

not_found: No independently verified procurement establishing installed-cost parity for a reinforcing system meeting the complete test was located.
No common external qualification threshold covering chloride, carbonation and stray-current exposures together was located.
Candidate-specific ASTM E119 floor qualification results were not located.
A public Caltrans material-acceptance record for Allium’s Long Valley Creek installation was not located.
The accessible ASTM A706/A706M-22a document contains a three-page excerpt.
The supplied IMPACT economic-impact page could not be retrieved.

results.finding: One full-size concrete slab reinforced with epoxy-coated bars achieved at least 4 hr, 10 min of fire endurance.
results.detail: The loaded, restrained slab was tested in accordance with ASTM E119. The abstract reports fire endurance but does not separately describe each acceptance criterion.
results.quote: As evidenced by the test results, the fire endurance of the slab reinforced with epoxy-coated bars is at least 4 hr, 10 min.
